extracted.intended_audience: litigators, in-house counsel, patent attorneys, and judges handling civil patent cases in the Republic of Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural and evidentiary guidance for conducting civil patent (and related IP) litigation in the Republic of Korea, including jurisdictional rules, case management, evidence production, expert use, preliminary injunctions, and trade-secret protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and access rules of the ECFS (electronic case filing system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties receive email and text notifications when the other party files documents; consenting defendants/respondents may receive electronic notices of the plaintiff’s/petitioner’s filings; judges and court officials may view case records electronically; electronic files are closed to the public and only litigants, their attorneys and the court can access them; the public may access published court decisions via the judiciary’s online decision search service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECFS enables prompt checking of case status, replacement of paper-based process, display of records during hearings. Parties should expect electronic submission and restricted public access; prepare filings and hearing materials in electronic formats (PDF, slideshow, video) as part of the court record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial jurisdiction for IP lawsuits (Article 24 of the Civil Procedure Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawsuit concerning IP rights (distinguishing between 'patent and other listed IP rights' and other IP) may be brought to specified district courts; lawsuits concerning patent and other listed IP rights are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court in the jurisdictional area of a high court (with concurrent original jurisdiction to the Seoul Central District Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Article 24 sets exclusive jurisdiction, agreement to the contrary is void; a court without jurisdiction will not become competent even if parties argue on the merits. Whether a case is a 'lawsuit concerning patent and other listed IP rights' is critical to jurisdictional determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Court jurisdiction under the Court Organization Act (Article 28-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court shall judge certain first-instance cases provided in patent-related statutes and appeals of cases under Article 24(2) and (3) of the Civil Procedure Act; it has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over lawsuits concerning patent and other listed IP rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive appellate jurisdiction is enforceable irrespective of subject matter jurisdiction; appeals of small claims patent cases also fall under the Patent Court. Parties should expect appeals in patent matters to be handled by the Patent Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claims considered 'concerning' patent and listed IP rights (scope of exclusive jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that typically require expert technical knowledge and thus fall under exclusive jurisdiction include injunctions against infringement, disposal/destruction, recovery of reputation, damages, transfer or extinguishment of patent registration, claims to establish/extinguish exclusive/nonexclusive licenses, remuneration for employee invention, royalty claims, and confirmation of attribution of IP rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts concentrate such cases to specialized courts to leverage judges' technical expertise; parties asserting or defending such claims should frame issues to show they involve technical matters requiring specialized adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of cases lacking jurisdiction (Article 36(3) Civil Procedure Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court lacking jurisdiction over a lawsuit concerning patent and other listed IP rights should transfer the case to a competent court; a competent court may also transfer a case to avoid significant damage or delay, either ex officio or on party request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal interpretation suggests Article 36(3) may not apply to appeals; there have been calls to allow discretionary transfer in appellate situations when significant damage or delay is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for preliminary injunctions (Article 303 Civil Execution Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunction cases may be brought to any district court having jurisdiction over the location of disputed subject matter, in addition to the district courts with exclusive jurisdiction for patent matters; the Patent Court is not competent to hear appeals of preliminary injunctions—such appeals go to the competent high court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions were left out of jurisdictional concentration; parties seeking provisional relief should plan filings in the district court having territorial connection to the disputed subject matter and anticipate a separate appellate route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter jurisdiction allocation (single judge vs panel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial power of a district court is exercised by a single judge in principle, but certain cases (Article 32(1)) are heard by a three-judge panel. Claims for monetary awards exceeding KRW 500 million go to a three-judge panel; multiple claims are summed to determine value; cases seeking injunctions or registration/transfer/extinguishment (where value cannot be calculated) go to district court panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A case originally assigned to a single judge may be taken by a panel court upon its decision. Parties should evaluate the monetary and non-monetary relief sought to anticipate bench composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction by court level / appellate paths
rubrics_metrics.description: For lawsuits concerning patent and other listed IP rights, the Patent Court has exclusive appellate jurisdiction. For appeals of other IP rights, appeals go either to a district court panel or the high court depending on first-instance composition. The Supreme Court is the court of last resort for all civil patent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should plan appeal strategy understanding that the Patent Court is the usual appellate forum for patent-listed IP appeals; Supreme Court remains ultimate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to submit written briefs in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must submit written briefs in advance so trials proceed in a focused manner; briefs should be filed in due time to give the other party a chance to prepare; a brief containing a new offensive or defensive method should be served at least seven days before the trial or preparatory hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is critical—late introduction of new theories risks exclusion. Plan briefing schedules to allow opponent preparation and court consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief content for inventive-step (obviousness) contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefs challenging inventive step should contain an element-by-element chart identifying elements in the prior art and comparing them with corresponding elements of the patented invention; when arguing lack of inventive step via combination of multiple prior arts, specify the primary prior art and explain how the prior arts are combined and why a PHOSITA could readily obtain that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear charts and detailed combination reasoning; unsupported or vague combination theories are weak. Use element mapping and rationale for combining references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief content for infringement contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefs should specify in detail, both individually and graphically, the product or process practiced by the defendant, listing product name and type/number and attaching drawings or pictures so the enforcing authority can identify them without further deliberation; include element-by-element comparison charts between the patented invention and the defendant's product/process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical and documentary specificity helps identification and comparison; describe accused product/process in detail to permit direct element matching and reduce need for court fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief content for damages contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant seeking compensatory damages should specify the legal provisions forming the basis for calculating damages and identify the exhibit number associated with each legal element; to dispute alleged facts, the other party should provide a detailed answer rather than a simple denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie factual allegations to statutory/legal elements and exhibits; bare denials are insufficient—provide documentary or factual rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early case management and trial scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the case is to be decided without trial, the presiding judge must set the trial date without delay, usually as soon as the defendant files an answer; the judge will evaluate dispute intensity, complexity, suitability for mediation, or urgency, and set the earliest practical trial date; cases likely to settle via mediation may be referred before the first trial date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate quick scheduling; consider early mediation and be prepared to explain complexity or need for expedited adjudication to influence scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses and purposes of preparatory hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparatory hearings sort out arguments and evidence to enable effective and focused trials; they are exceptional and used in complex civil patent cases (often via video conference) to coordinate case management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical matters discussed: trial date/time; issues to be addressed; deadlines for stating contentions and submitting evidence (including expert affidavits), maximum number and length of submissions; use and deadlines for time-consuming evidence production methods (inspection, appraisal, expert witnesses); designation of technical advisor; whether to hold technology review sessions; separate hearings by legal issue; coordination with related IPTAB cases; referrals to mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between main suit and petition for provisional disposition (preliminary injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two civil actions: main suit (permanent injunction and damages) and petition for provisional disposition (preliminary injunction only, damages not recoverable in that proceeding). Preliminary injunctions are relatively quick methods for enforcing IP rights but have stricter requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff seeking preliminary relief must show likelihood of infringement and necessity for provisional relief, and should expect limited discovery and documentary-evidence-focused proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for granting a preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction will not be granted merely because the patent is shown to be valid and infringed; plaintiff must demonstrate likelihood of infringement and necessity for provisional relief. Courts balance irreparable harm to plaintiff against economic harm to defendant, consider adequacy of relief, and likelihood of patent invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare strong documentary evidence of infringement and arguments on irreparable harm and necessity; anticipate the court weighing invalidity risk and adequacy of non-injunctive remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and discovery expectations in preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial hearing typically scheduled within two to three weeks of filing; evidence of infringement should be submitted (brochures, samples); witness testimony is usually limited to affidavits; very little discovery is allowed; courts are often reluctant to grant injunctions requiring expert testimony or tests; documentary evidence is primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather documentary proof and samples before filing; reliance on extensive expert testing risks denial; use affidavits and concrete product materials where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and remedies connected to preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: If granted, injunction remedies include prohibiting manufacture/sale, ordering transfer/custody/destruction of infringing articles, or public notice orders; courts generally require plaintiff to post security deposit/bond to cover damages if injunction later overturned; plaintiff may be liable for tort (ordinary and foreseeable extraordinary damages) if injunction improperly issued, and is rebuttably presumed negligent if injunction improperly issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh risks and costs of posting bond and potential liability; defendants may request revocation or request the court to compel plaintiff to file a main suit and failure to do so can lead to revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: General evidence production framework (no US-style pre-trial discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil Procedure Act does not provide depositions/interrogatories like the US; evidence is produced during trials; in exceptional cases, a party may request a court order to examine evidence prior to filing; all requests for evidence production are petitions to the court and the court balances need for evidence against delay/harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must specify in detail the matters to be substantiated; plan early preservation and petitions when evidence is in other parties’ possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary evidence requirements and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable documentary evidence includes patent specifications, technical literature, published materials, patent gazettes/registers, and products/models/photos/videos; documentary evidence should be original in principle but scanned versions are generally acceptable unless authenticity is disputed; foreign-language documents must be submitted with translations (except permitted language in international cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File originals or be ready to produce originals if authenticity challenged; provide certified translations where required; include multimedia and product samples when relevant to technical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection (product/sample and on-site inspection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may ask the court to inspect samples of another party’s products or conduct on-site inspection of premises; petitioners may request that the court order the product be submitted for inspection; the court may inspect directly or appoint an expert to inspect and report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must persuade the court of necessity for inspection (e.g., manufacturing process evidence); be prepared for court-appointed experts to accompany inspections and submit findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-appointed expert evaluation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Court can appoint independent experts to provide opinions on complex technical issues (Article 335); experts may be appointed at party request or at the court’s discretion; the court may seek opinions from public institutions; parties may petition to disqualify experts for bias or lack of qualification; experts must take an oath and may be permitted to enter premises with court approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect broad court discretion in selection/denial; if recommending an expert, anticipate potential objections and supply evidence of fairness and qualifications; court-appointed expert opinions carry institutional weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document submission orders under Civil Procedure Act
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may petition the court to order another party or third party to submit a document relevant to the merits (Article 343); the petition must indicate document title, purpose, holder, facts the document proves and basis for obligation; the holder must produce the document under specified conditions (e.g., party has referred to it, petitioner entitled to perusal, document made for petitioner’s benefit or concerning legal relationship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft petitions with detailed identification and legal basis; expect the court to enforce production when statutory criteria are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material submission orders under the Patent Act (expanded scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act expands submission orders from 'documents' to 'materials' (including electronic files, video clips, nondocumentary data) and limits refusal based on trade secrets; petitioning party may use in camera proceedings to show trade-secret character, but holder cannot simply refuse; court may limit disclosure scope or persons with access; if material is unjustifiably withheld, court may presume the requested facts true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material submission orders to obtain non-documentary evidence; prepare to request in camera trade-secret review and seek protective measures; defendants must be prepared to present evidence of their actual process/product if a prima facie showing of infringement is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for accused infringer to respond with evidence when prima facie infringement shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning July 9, 2019, accused patent or utility-model infringers must respond to credible infringement claims with evidence rather than simple denials; if a prima facie showing of likely infringement is made and the accused denies infringement, they must present evidence of the actual process or product practiced or risk the court presuming infringement occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants should maintain and be ready to produce process/product evidence; plaintiffs should assemble prima facie evidence to trigger the burden shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-preservation petitions (before or during infringement action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners seeking evidence preservation must establish likelihood/reasonable probability of patent infringement and necessity for preservation; successful petitions yield rulings specifying subject, place, date of examination, facts to be proven and subject materials. Before filing suit, petitions go to the district court for the place of residence of the party possessing evidence or location of the evidence; after filing, petitions go to the court where the lawsuit was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence-preservation to secure items otherwise difficult to obtain; craft petitions to show necessity and connect to likely infringement; expect single-judge review pre-suit and the same panel post-filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witnesses (roles, submission and testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert witnesses in patent cases testify on matters like the technical level of a PHOSITA at filing, disclosure of prior art, analysis/comparison of infringing goods, amount of loss and reasonable royalty. Petitioners must submit a 'Basic Statement for Expert Witness'; expert opinion may be submitted via declaration (common) or direct testimony; questions for direct testimony must be submitted in writing; court discretion governs admission and other party may cross-examine if testimony allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare Basic Statement and expert declarations in advance; expect the court to prefer written expert declarations; if calling live experts, prepare written questions and be ready for cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial technical examiners (court-employed technical support)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court and some IP divisions have judicial technical examiners who provide full-time support through specialized examination of technical matters; they often have scientific/technical backgrounds (KIPO examiners, patent attorneys, researchers) and may participate in preparatory hearings and trials and hold technical explanatory sessions before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial technical examiners help the bench understand technical issues—parties should be prepared to explain technologies in accessible formats and can use technical explanatory sessions to aid judges’ technical comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical advisors (court-appointed external experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may appoint technical advisors from a pool of registered experts (researchers, professors) to provide written opinions or attend trials to explain technical matters and, with judge permission, ask questions. They are bound by confidentiality and deemed government employees for bribery provisions. They differ from judicial technical examiners by being outside professionals appointed case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider requesting qualified technical advisors when specific expertise is needed; be prepared to provide technical materials and accommodate confidentiality obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology tutorials and technical briefing sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial panels hold pre-trial internal technical explanatory sessions to understand technologies; on the trial date, technology review sessions may be held where parties present oral arguments and technical presentations (drawings, videos, photos); parties are advised to submit technology-review materials prior to trial (PDF/slideshow/video) which become part of the court record; parties may electronically submit files before trial, and trials may be conducted in a foreign language with consent and court approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare visual and multimedia technical presentations, submit them in the recommended electronic formats in advance, and coordinate for any foreign-language needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited access to trade secrets in court records
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon request, the court can order that only the parties to the lawsuit may access or copy portions of the court record containing trade secrets or require delivery of authentic/certified copies or abstracts of the portions containing trade secrets in decisions or trial records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use court orders to limit public access to trade-secret material within court records; recognize that such orders do not by themselves prevent parties from disclosing trade secrets outside litigation and additional protective orders may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality protective orders for trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may refuse to produce a document claiming it contains confidential information; the court may order an in camera review (parties and counsel excluded). Under Article 14-4 of the Unfair Competition Prevention and Trade Secret Protection Act, a party may petition for a confidentiality protective order to prevent unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets in litigation alleging unfair competition/trade-secret violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek confidentiality protective orders and in camera review to limit disclosure scope; expect procedures that restrict access and permit limited dissemination consistent with protecting trade secrets.
